teaser: A wall of gold, painted on both sides, that a whole city carried through its streets.
review_notes:
Image is a digital reconstruction of the FRONT of the altarpiece (main panel + predella + pinnacles on a black background), not a photo of the object as displayed in the museum. The top-center pinnacle shown is a hypothetical filler: the original central pinnacle panels are lost.
Original overall height 'about five meters (16 feet)' is the usual scholarly estimate, please verify.
Main panel size given as about 2.1 x 4 m (213 x 396 cm).
Procession on June 9, 1311 with shops closed and bells ringing: from a contemporary Sienese chronicle.
Contract dated 1308.
Duccio's fines (debts, breaking curfew, refusing military service): from Sienese archives, wording simplified.
Back: 26 Passion scenes on the main panel.
Removed from high altar in 1506; sawn apart in 1771.
Museums holding dispersed panels: National Gallery London, Frick Collection New York, National Gallery of Art Washington, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza Madrid, Kimbell Art Museum Fort Worth.
Inscription translation is a standard paraphrase of MATER SANCTA DEI SIS CAUSA SENIS REQUIEI SIS DUCIO VITA TE QUIA PINXIT ITA.

lesson.text: Begin with the wood. Poplar planks, glued and nailed into a wall about five meters high (16 feet), then covered on both faces with paint and real gold. When it left Duccio's workshop in June 1311, Siena had never seen a painting this big.

The image in front of you rebuilds the front as it once stood. In the middle, the main panel, roughly 2.1 by 4 meters (7 by 13 feet). Below it runs a strip of small stories called a predella, the base of an altarpiece. On top, a crown of pointed gables.

On June 9, 1311, Siena closed its shops for the day. The bishop, the priests, the city officials and a crowd holding candles walked the finished painting from the workshop to the cathedral while every bell in town rang.

Why such a fuss over a painting? Siena considered the Virgin Mary its personal protector. Half a century earlier, before a battle against Florence that it had little chance of winning, the city had handed her its keys. It won. A “Maestà”, Italian for “majesty”, shows her as a queen on her throne, holding court.

So this is a state portrait as much as a religious one, and the painter knew how much it mattered. Artists of his time almost never signed their work. Duccio did, and he chose the most visible spot he could without touching the holy figures.
Duccio wrote his own name on this painting. Where would a painter dare to put it?

spots.title: The step of the throne
spots.text: A band of red letters runs around the base, right under Mary's feet. It is a prayer in Latin, and Duccio's name is inside it.

lesson.text: The prayer says, roughly: Holy Mother of God, give Siena peace, and give Duccio life, because he painted you like this. One line for the city, one line for himself. A craftsman, paid by the day, is asking for a reward in the same breath as his government.
With the Maestà, a painter stops being an anonymous workman. He signs, he bargains with heaven, and a whole city walks behind his work.

The paint is tempera: colored powder mixed with egg yolk. It dries in minutes, so there is no blending on the panel. Every soft cheek is built from hundreds of hair-thin strokes. The background is gold leaf, real gold beaten thinner than paper, then polished with a smooth stone until it shines like metal.

Now the hard part. Duccio has to fit a queen, a child, a throne and a crowd of angels and saints into one rectangle, and it must stay calm enough to pray in front of. His answer is almost architectural.
Three simple lines hold this whole crowd in order.

lines.label: The axis
lines.text: Mary sits exactly in the middle, and far larger than anyone else. In medieval painting, size shows rank, not distance.

lines.label: Rows of halos
lines.text: Angels and saints stand in ranks, heads at the same height like a choir. The gold discs repeat across the panel as a steady rhythm.

lines.label: The kneeling four
lines.text: Four figures kneel in front, two on each side. They are Siena's own patron saints, placed nearest to us, speaking to Mary for the city.

lesson.text: That strict order comes from Byzantine art, the style of icons from the eastern Mediterranean: gold, symmetry, stillness. What Duccio adds is softness. Heads tilt. Angels lean their chins on the throne like children at a windowsill. The gold edge of Mary's dark cloak wanders down her body in one loose, curling line.
Siena's archives show Duccio being fined again and again: for debts, for breaking the curfew, for refusing to turn up for military service. The city kept giving him its biggest commissions anyway.

Remember the two painted faces. The back, not shown here, carried the Passion, the last days of Jesus, in 26 scenes. Citizens in the nave saw the queen. The priests, seated behind the altar, saw the story. The contract of 1308 gave Duccio one job only, and he spent about three years on it.

Even on the front, the edges are full of stories. The strip below tells the childhood of Jesus, each scene separated by a prophet holding a scroll. The gables above tell the last days of Mary. Wander through them.

spots.title: The Annunciation
spots.text: The story begins at the far left: an angel steps through an archway to tell Mary she will have a child. The little building is tilted to show us its inside.

spots.title: A prophet
spots.text: Between two scenes stands a man with a scroll. Prophets from the Old Testament act as footnotes, announcing what the next picture shows.

spots.title: The Nativity
spots.text: Mary lies on a red cushion in a cave under a wooden shelter. She is still the biggest figure, even lying down.

spots.title: The Child
spots.text: Wrapped in a thin pink cloth, he sits on his mother's arm like a real, heavy baby. Her hand closes around his leg to hold him.

spots.title: Leaning angels
spots.text: Angels rest on the back of the marble throne and peer over it. A small, human gesture inside a very formal picture.

spots.title: A kneeling bishop
spots.text: One of Siena's four patron saints, in a white and gold robe, with his bishop's staff. He looks up at Mary on the city's behalf.

spots.title: Mary's last days
spots.text: In the gables, the apostles gather around Mary's bed. These scenes close the story that the strip at the bottom opened.

spots.title: Gable angels
spots.text: At the very top, an angel in each pointed frame. The gilded spires echo the Gothic cathedral the painting was made for.

lesson.text: In those small scenes Duccio is freest. Rooms open like doll houses, people argue, sleep, travel. Younger Sienese painters such as Simone Martini and the Lorenzetti brothers learned storytelling from these panels, and Siena's gentle, colorful manner stayed recognizable for two centuries.

The painting's own story is rougher. In 1506 it was taken down from the high altar, out of fashion. In 1771 it was sawn apart: front split from back, big panels cut into pieces, small ones sold off one by one.
Pieces of the Maestà now hang in London, New York, Washington, Madrid and Fort Worth, Texas. A few panels have never been found, so nobody alive has seen the whole thing.

quiz.question: What does the Italian word “Maestà” mean?
quiz.explanation: A Maestà shows Mary in majesty, as a queen on her throne holding court.

quiz.question: Where did Duccio put his name?
options: On the step of the throne, inside a prayer
On a scroll held by a prophet
On the back of a gable
quiz.explanation: The red Latin inscription under Mary's feet asks for peace for Siena and life for Duccio.

quiz.question: What is tempera?
quiz.explanation: Tempera binds colored powder with egg yolk and dries within minutes.

quiz.question: Who are the four figures kneeling in front?
options: The men who paid for the painting
quiz.explanation: They are the city's own patron saints, speaking to Mary on its behalf.

quiz.question: What was painted on the back?
options: The Passion of Jesus in many small scenes
quiz.explanation: The back told the Passion in 26 scenes for the priests seated behind the altar.

facts.text: The Maestà was carried to the cathedral in a procession while the city's shops stayed closed.
facts.explanation: On June 9, 1311, Siena stopped work and walked the painting through the streets.

facts.text: In the main panel, Mary is the same size as the saints around her.
facts.explanation: She is far larger: in medieval painting, size shows rank.

facts.text: Today the whole altarpiece can be seen together in Siena.
facts.explanation: It was sawn apart in 1771 and its pieces are spread across several countries, with some lost.
